Flood Insurance Data

The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county

In plain words

Of NFIP (federal flood insurance) policies in force on August 31, 2026 on single-family primary homes with both premiums recorded, 36.2% pay a premium at least $100 a year below the full-risk premium FEMA records for the same policy. In the median listed county it is 29.0%. FEMA defines the full-risk premium as “The chargeable premium for a property based on its determined flood risk and the full cost to pay anticipated losses and expenses for that property.”

Find your county (1,793 listed; a county with fewer than 30 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways is not):

In FEMA's records for policies in force, 36.2% of 2,320,347 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways across all U.S. counties combined had a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium; across the 1,793 counties with at least 30 each, 36.2% (90% range 33.3–39.0%, resampling counties).

By Michael Woo, publisher of Flood Insurance Data (about the site), who works with data, is not an insurance agent, adjuster or engineer, and answers for every figure here. Written with AI tools; every row is recomputed from FEMA's records by a separate check before publishing.

Abstract

Data: 1,793 counties with at least 30 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways each (2,307,620 in all), from FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3, policies in force, as of August 31, 2026.

Result: across those counties, 36.2% (90% range 33.3–39.0%, resampling counties) of single-family primary-home policies priced both ways had a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium; the median county's share is 29.0%. The highest share is Pike County, IL at 95.4% (62 of 65); the lowest share, 0.0%, is shared by 19 counties.

Question

In which U.S. counties do NFIP single-family primary homes most often pay a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium for the same policy, and how large is the gap there? The measure is the share of NFIP single-family primary-home policies in force whose premium is at least $100 a year below the full-risk premium FEMA records on the same policy.

The $100 line is this paper's choice, so that a gap of a few dollars is not counted as a price gap; the share below by any amount and the median gap are in the table, and Results gives the pooled share by any amount, by $10 or more and by $100 or more, so a reader can see how much the line moves the figure.

Data

FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3 (API) records as of August 31, 2026, FEMA fields totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy, fullRiskPremium, crsClassCode, policyCount, occupancyType, primaryResidenceIndicator, condominiumCoverageTypeCode, censusGeoid. Base: NFIP policies in force on the data date on single-family primary homes (FEMA occupancy type 1 or 11, primary residence, condominium coverage type N or blank) with a premium above $0 and a full-risk premium above $0 (refunds and blanks left out); the gap is full-risk premium minus premium, both premium only, before fees and surcharges; counted as records, and every such single-family record here holds one policy unit, which the check confirms.

FEMA defines fullRiskPremium as "The chargeable premium for a property based on its determined flood risk and the full cost to pay anticipated losses and expenses for that property."

FEMA defines totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy as "Total Insurance Premium of the Policy in whole dollars. Negative values indicate a refund."

FEMA defines crsClassCode as "The Community Rating System (CRS) Classification Credit Percentage used to rate the policy." and adds "Beginning with Risk Rating 2.0, there are no longer percentage discount differences for policies inside and outside of the SFHA."

FEMA defines policyCount as "Insured units in an active status."

Methods

The share is the number of single-family primary-home policies priced both ways that had a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium, divided by all single-family primary-home policies priced both ways in the county FEMA codes on the record, both counted from the same records. A county is listed only with at least 30 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways. Left out: 1,140 counties with fewer than 30 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways and 94 with none; across the 1,140 left-out counties with at least one, the median share of premiums $100 or more below full-risk is 30.0% and the pooled share 34.8%, so the listed counties are not a sample of every county. Intervals, fifths, the county-resampling range, records left out and why no test is run: shared methods for every paper.

Results

  • Pooled over the 1,793 counties: 36.2% (90% range 33.3–39.0%) of 2,307,620 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways; the 1,140 counties left out pool to 34.8%.
  • The line moves the figure: pooled over the 1,793 counties, 43.7% of 2,307,620 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways are below full-risk by any amount, 42.6% by $10 or more and 36.2% by $100 or more.
  • By the CRS class code FEMA records on the policy (classes with 1,000 or more policies here; descriptive, no test), the share below by any amount is class 2 39.7% of 29,851; class 3 55.8% of 139,767; class 4 32.3% of 35,279; class 5 45.9% of 635,777; class 6 38.6% of 242,601; class 7 42.3% of 430,139; class 8 46.2% of 144,107; class 9 54.4% of 47,961; class 10 52.4% of 49,087; no class code 39.8% of 552,095.
  • Median county: 29.0%. Highest: Pike County, IL, 95.4% (90% range 89.0–98.1%).
  • 19 of the 50 counties with the highest share of premiums $100 or more below full-risk are in West Virginia, which has 44 of the 1,793 listed counties.

Prior work

Published work on this measure, read 2026-11-14: GAO's report GAO-27-108012 (October 1, 2026) gives, for every county with at least 10 properties and as a download, the percentage of all NFIP policies in a county with premiums that do not fully reflect their flood risk as of April 2026, by any amount, with no count of policies and no size of the gap. Neptune Flood's research group reports 1.5 million policyholders, 42% of the program, still paying below their full-risk price, about $2.6 billion a year; Neptune's 42% counts every NFIP policyholder, while this paper's share below by any amount counts only single-family primary homes priced both ways, so the two shares are on different bases. This paper differs in base (single-family primary homes only), in a material line (at least $100 a year, with the any-amount share beside it), in giving the gap's size, the policy count and a 90% range for every county, and in the CRS split. GAO-27-108012 interactive county map and data download. Neptune Flood analysis as reported by InsuranceNewsNet. Collier County, FL: here 82.2% of 31,301 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways are below full-risk by any amount and 80.1% by $100 or more, as of August 31, 2026; GAO's download gives 0.765 (76.5%) of all NFIP policies there as of April 2026; the two differ in base (all policies against single-family primary homes) and date.

Download all 1,793 rows as CSV (14 columns: fifth, county_fips, county, state, share_pct, ci90_low_pct, ci90_high_pct, numerator, denominator, in_force_on, as_of, below_any_amount_n, below_any_amount_pct, median_gap_usd_below_any_amount). share_pct, ci90_low_pct, ci90_high_pct and numerator count policies at least $100 a year below full-risk; below_any_amount_n, below_any_amount_pct and median_gap_usd_below_any_amount count policies below by any amount (the median gap is blank where fewer than 30 are below).

Limitations

  • FEMA's data dictionary does not say whether the full-risk premium is before or after the Community Rating System credit; Results gives the share by the CRS class code on the policy so a reader can see whether the class lines up with the share.
  • The data does not say which discount puts a premium below full-risk (the yearly increase cap, pre-flood-map construction, a newly mapped area or another rule), and this paper does not say either.
  • The gap is a yearly premium difference on one snapshot of policies in force; it is not what any one owner will pay next year.
  • The median gap is over every policy below full-risk by any amount, and is printed only where 30 or more policies are below.
  • Counties come from the census geography FEMA codes on each policy (censusGeoid), which can differ from the property's county.
  • The table is ordered by share alone, not by count: a county with few policies can sit above a county with thousands whose 90% range overlaps its own, so counties within one fifth cannot be told apart and the order inside a fifth is not a ranking.
  • Policies in one county share a flood map, a community and its rating, so they are not independent; each county's 90% range treats them as independent and is narrower than it should be.
  • Every listed county gets its own 90% range, so about one range in ten would be expected to miss that county's true share by chance alone; no range is adjusted for the number of counties.
  • Only NFIP records: private flood insurance is not in FEMA's data.
  • A fifth is a position in this list, not a grade, a risk score or a prediction.

Reproduce

Download every record from FEMA OpenFEMA NFIP Policies v3, keep the single-family primary-home policies priced both ways in force on the data date, group by the county FEMA codes, count the base and the records meeting the measure, drop counties under 30, and compute each share of premiums $100 or more below full-risk with a 90% Wilson interval (z = 1.64485), checking against the CSV, which gives every numerator and denominator.
